newsitem.title: GERMANY: Further pay deals seen in German metal sector.
newsitem.headline: Further pay deals seen in German metal sector.

text.p: Further wage deal covering most of Germany's metal and engineering sector were expected on Monday after a break-through pact was reached last Thursday between employers and workers in the state of Lower Saxony.

The Lower Saxony deal means an average labour cost increase of less than one percent for companies in the state, but was seen as an embarassing defeat for employers because it fails to implement a new law making a 20 percent cut to sick pay costs.

IG Metall, the powerful trade union that has been leading worker protests against the sick pay cuts, said it was now hopeful a wage deal could be signed for the 850,000 employees in the steel-making region of North Rhine-Westphalia.
A spokeswoman for IG Metall in Dortmund said in response to enquiries the union was confident that there too, sick payments would be maintained at the current 100 percent of salary.
IG Metall hailed the Lower Saxony agreement, which itself only applies to some 90,000 workers, as a break-through after protests that have involved hundreds of thousands of workers in the sector.
An official for the North Rhine-Westphalian metal and engineering employers federation said it was expecting a deal before Christmas, without adding what kind of wage package it was ready to offer.

Employer representatives in the large southern state of Bavaria said they were now looking for quick agreement on a package similar to the Lower Saxony deal, which they nonetheless said was not completely satisfactory.
Under the Lower Saxony package, workers will receive a 1.5 percent rise in 1997 salaries and a 2.5 percent increase in 1998.
In return for maintaining full sick pay, workers have agreed to lower Christmas bonuses.

An IG Metall spokeswoman in Stuttgart had earlier said union leaders there were also expecting to sign a deal similar to the Lower Saxony pact for some 300,000 workers in the southern part of the state of Baden-Wuerttemberg.
The new agreements, if signed, will mean that the majority of wage contracts for the 3.2 million workers in the metal and engineering industry will have been settled for 1997.
